digest.definition: An interdisciplinary, multi-professional field, first offered as degrees in 1992, that studies children from conception to eight and educates those who work with them and their families
distinctiveFeatures: An interdisciplinary, multi-professional field, first offered as degrees in 1992, that studies children from conception to eight and educates those who work with them and their families
It draws on health, education, social work, psychology, sociology, philosophy, history, cultural, legal and political studies, economics and neuroscience
Holism is its organising idea: development, well-being, participation and learning seen together and in context, with play central
It speaks of many childhoods, not one, and treats childhood as contested and changing, read locally, nationally and globally
It is committed to social justice, children's rights and advocacy, and asks graduates to act as agents of change
Theory and practice are linked throughout; placements are common but optional, and the Level 6 practitioner competencies are an optional route
Research, enquiry and reflexivity run through it, including ethical study of young children

subjectSpecific.text: You will be able to reflect on how psychology, sociology, health, history, education and philosophy each shape the way babies, young children and childhood are understood.
You will be able to bring several perspectives to early childhood questions, aware that the field uses varied methods, theories, evidence and applications.
You will be able to observe and analyse aspects of babies' and young children's lives, with reasonable adjustments for accessibility where needed.
You will be able to combine ideas and findings from the field's many perspectives and see how each treats an issue in its own way.
You will be able to critique constructively the theory, practice and research on children's development, well-being, participation and learning across diverse childhoods.
You will be able to show knowledge and awareness of the skills that different pedagogical approaches call for.
You will be able to understand how deep and strong relationships need to be with individual babies and children and with groups, and how to help children build relationships with each other.
You will be able to build and encourage relationships of mutual respect with families, colleagues, other professionals and communities.
You will be able to evaluate and develop your own values about teaching and care.
You will be able to reflect on why the natural world and time outdoors matter for how all young children and their families grow, develop, know and understand.

You will be able to explore, examine and judge critically the cultural, historical and current features of policies, institutions and agencies, local to global, and what they mean for children's development and for ideas of childhood.
You will be able to show a strong grasp of the pedagogy of play as several disciplines see it.
You will be able to plan, and where fitting carry out, curriculum, assessment, evaluation and improvement of creative learning, with regard to children's health and emotional well-being.
You will be able to lead, support and collaborate with others and understand effective teamwork with parents, carers and other professionals.
You will be able to understand how to plan for, and where fitting deliver, the protection, safety, health and well-being of children and the conditions in which they thrive.
You will be able to build critical arguments for improving multiagency and multi-professional practice for babies and young children.
You will be able to observe and analyse aspects of babies' and young children's lives.
You will be able to reflect on the ethics of studying babies, young children, their families and communities.
You will be able to form and test out hypotheses and research questions on early childhood, seen in its ecological context.
You will be able to carry out ethical empirical studies with varied data collection, observation of early childhood in its ecological context among them, and analyse the data.
You will be able to present and judge research findings on early childhood.
You will be able to understand critically how political, economic, cultural and ideological contexts, from local to global, act on one another in the lives of children, families and communities.
You will be able to recognise and challenge inequality in society and take an anti-bias approach.
You will be able to recognise children's agency, help their voices be heard and, where fitting, advocate for babies, young children, families and communities.

transferable.text: You will be able to present information in suitable forms, online or offline, with a sense of audience.
You will be able to show empathy and active listening and develop ways to guard against burnout from emotional labour.
You will be able to give and defend an informed view, drawing on a range of theoretical positions.
You will be able to understand data and use it well.
You will be able to communicate with others and reflect on your own and others' skills, beliefs, understanding and views.
You will be able to frame and sharpen questions and judge critically.
You will be able to weigh different perspectives critically and reach well-supported conclusions.
You will be able to find, retrieve, organise and use varied information sources, primary sources among them, and judge critically how relevant they are.
You will be able to engage with research and practice and with the uncertainty of knowledge still being built.
You will be able to use communication skills to talk, debate, negotiate, persuade and challenge others' ideas, with reasonable adjustments for disabled students where needed.
You will be able to lead and collaborate with others with insight and confidence.
You will be able to be alert to contextual and interpersonal factors, seeing how complex influences shape behaviour and interaction and give rise to problems and conflict.
You will be able to see the value of cooperation in making individual skills more effective.
You will be able to write for varied purposes, such as persuading, explaining, describing, evaluating, recounting, summarising and hypothesising.
You will be able to evaluate and analyse critically.
You will be able to use digital technology and social media appropriately in different contexts and reflect on that use.
You will be able to become a learner who works autonomously, growing in independence, resilience, responsibility and pragmatism.

statements.paraphrase: Undergraduates and postgraduates should keep questioning the language, assumptions and entrenched dominant ways of thinking in ideas of knowledge and power; agency, equal rights and dignity ground social justice, and equality is both an ethical matter and a human right.

forPractitioner.text: Students at every level should be helped to keep questioning dominant ways of thinking about knowledge and power, with equality treated as an ethical and human-rights question that underpins anti-oppressive practice.

statements.about: teaching that challenges dominant knowledge; institutional support
statements.paraphrase: Students at all levels meet teaching that challenges dominant knowledge and gives marginalised voices more room; they will be pushed to think critically and make their own pedagogical judgements with equality in mind, and institutions will show active systems of support.

forPractitioner.text: Teaching will challenge dominant knowledge and widen representation; students will be pushed to make their own pedagogical judgements with EDI in mind, and the institution will have proactive, inclusive support in place.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be stretched to question different realities critically and reach your own judgements about teaching and care, keeping equality and inclusion in view, with support from your institution.

statements.about: equitable courses, critical reflection and placements from birth to eight
statements.paraphrase: Every degree will be meaningful, fair and grounded in scholarship and practice under social justice, and will respect each student's identity and knowledge; courses should foster personal and theoretical critical reflection across theories, practice from birth to eight and disciplines; placements meant to qualify students for early years practice must comply with each nation's guidance, while students should still gain experience across the age range and across health, social care and education.

forPractitioner.text: Courses will be equitable and respect what each student brings, and should build critical reflection across theory, practice from birth to eight and disciplines. Placements that qualify students for early years practice must meet the guidance of the student's nation, and students should still gain experience across ages and across health, social care and education.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course will respect who you are and what you bring, and should help you reflect critically on theory and practice from birth to eight; you should gain placement experience across that age range and across health, social care and education.

statements.appliesTo: courses that offer work-based or placement learning
statements.paraphrase: Where courses offer work-based or placement learning, it must be clearly defined, mentored, monitored, accessible and supervised, so that students learn how theory and practice connect in inclusive work with children and families across disciplines.

forPractitioner.text: Any placement or work-based element you offer must be clearly scoped, mentored, monitored, accessible and supervised, so that it teaches the link between theory and inclusive practice.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course that offers placements

statements.about: exploring sustainability, social justice and advocacy
statements.paraphrase: Drawing on the joint QAA and Advance HE sustainability guidance, students weigh the values behind ecological sustainability and can help children and communities grasp them; degrees should offer chances to explore sustainability, social justice, democratic action and advocacy from the personal to the global, so graduates show how ecology and sustainable societies link through social justice.

forPractitioner.text: The course should give students chances to explore sustainability, social justice, democratic action and advocacy at personal, professional, community, national and global scales, so that they can show how ecology and social justice connect.

forBeneficiary.text: You should have chances to explore sustainability, social justice, democracy and advocacy, from your own life to the global scale, and to show how caring for the planet and fairness in society connect.

statements.appliesTo: students and graduates of the subject
statements.paraphrase: Students and graduates help build a workforce that leads innovation and changes practice, relationships, settings and services; ready for change, they will be well placed to add social, cultural and economic value, and they work together to develop the sector and its standing through exchanging knowledge and practice.
